attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, in a parenthetical aside about OpenAI's May 2024 voice demo.

semantics.note: The drafter drops the hedge 'I daresay', which means roughly 'I suppose it's probable'. That is graded confidence, like 'I suspect', not a firm commitment. The normalised proposition states the claim without that qualifier, which overstates what Marcus committed to.

contract.note: The contract scores the claim on a plain reading, but plain reading applies only to firm language. 'I daresay' marks a hedged prediction, so scoring it as a firm forecast is unfair. 'Robustly' and the advertised capability set are also evaluator readings the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: OpenAI's May 13, 2024 announcement shows what was advertised. It does not test reliability.
OpenAI's June 2025 release notes admit ongoing voice hallucinations and audio-quality problems. These are company disclosures about a finite period and cannot show the claim 'never'.
OpenAI's July 2026 GPT-Live launch post is a company disclosure about a successor model. It is not independent, repeated reliability testing.
A single firsthand Tom's Guide test of translation and pause handling. It reports successes but is not repeatable testing across the full advertised scope.

reviews.rationale: 'I daresay' hedges the prediction with probability language, so under the policy it is not scored. Even read as a firm forecast, it would be unresolved: there is no deadline, failures over a finite period cannot prove 'never', and the packet has no independent repeated testing that would contradict it (e3 is a company disclosure, e4 is one anecdotal review).
